## What you will learn

- That an uncalibrated wide lens misplaces the **corner of every frame by 362 pixels — 7.5 metres
  on the ground at 60 m**
- That the error grows as the **cube of the radius**, so anything you check in the middle of the
  image looks perfect
- The nine intrinsic unknowns, and why **the principal point is never the centre of the sensor**
- Why you must **tilt the board**: a head-on plane cannot separate focal length from distance, and
  a hundred square-on images converge beautifully on the wrong answer
- How big a board you need at each distance, and the **focus-breathing trap** of calibrating at
  1 m and flying at 60
- That reprojection error converts straight into ground metres, and **0.30 px is the target**
- That **one degree of mount angle is 21× worse than a 5 cm lever arm** at 60 m — measure the
  angle, not the offset
- Why undistortion is an iteration, and why the same iteration fails on a fisheye

## Why it matters

[14.01](14.01-cameras-for-uavs.md) derived every geometric number from the pixel pitch and the
focal length, and quietly assumed the lens was a pinhole. It is not. Level 1 prices that
assumption and the number is startling: **7.5 metres on the ground**, in the corner of every
frame, on a camera you paid a few hundred shekels for and are about to trust with a survey.

Where it hurts is the part nobody looks at. Distortion is zero at the centre and grows as the cube
of the radius, so every check you do by eye — is that line straight, does that building look
right — is done in the region that was already fine. The damage is in the corners, and in a survey
the corners are exactly where adjacent images overlap.

It also matters because calibration is the cheapest accuracy you will ever buy. No hardware, no
subscription, an hour of your time and a printed board. [13.03](../13-navigation-gnss/13.03-rtk-and-ppk.md)
offered centimetres for ₪2,000; this offers metres for nothing, and if you have not done it, RTK
is improving a term that is not your problem.

> [!WARNING]
> Calibration is only valid for the camera you calibrated, in the state you calibrated it.
> A knock, a refocus, a lens swap, a different resolution mode, or a mount re-tightened at a
> different torque all invalidate it. Write the date on the file, and re-do it after anything that
> could have moved the lens. An out-of-date calibration is worse than none, because you will trust
> it.

## Concept

Hold a ruler up behind a cheap magnifying glass and look at the edges. The middle is fine; the
edges bow. That bowing is radial distortion, and every wide lens has it — it is not a defect, it
is the price of a wide field of view in a small package.

Calibration is the process of measuring that bowing precisely enough to undo it. You photograph
something whose geometry you already know — a printed checkerboard, whose squares are all the same
measured size — and you solve for the set of camera parameters that best explains the pictures you
got. What is left unexplained is the reprojection error, and it is the only honest score you get.

The subtle part is *why* you have to wave the board around. A flat target photographed head-on is
scale-ambiguous: a long lens far away and a short lens close up produce literally the same image.
No amount of data resolves that, because there is nothing in the pictures to resolve it with.
Tilting the board introduces perspective — one edge genuinely nearer than the other — and
perspective depends on focal length and distance differently. **The tilt is not a nicety; it is
what makes the problem solvable.**

The last idea is that intrinsics are only half of what you need. They describe the camera as an
instrument. They say nothing about where it is bolted or which way it points, and for turning a
pixel into a ground coordinate the mounting matters more than you would expect — by a factor of
twenty.

## Technical explanation

### Level 1 — what an uncalibrated lens costs

Run the code. Dividing the focal length by the pixel pitch gives the focal length **in pixels**,
$f_x = 2917.3$ px, which is what every vision equation actually uses.

Now walk out from the centre of the frame with a Brown–Conrady model using coefficients typical of
a wide 1/2.3" module **[S]**. A quarter of the way out, 7.0 px. Halfway, 54.0 px. Three quarters,
169.3 px. **At the corner, 362.5 pixels — 7.46 metres on the ground at 60 m.**

That is not a refinement. [13.03](../13-navigation-gnss/13.03-rtk-and-ppk.md) sold you centimetres
for ₪2,000, and an uncalibrated lens throws away seven metres in the corner of every frame — for
free, silently, and worst exactly where adjacent survey images overlap
([12.02](../12-autonomous-flight/12.02-mission-planning.md)).

Notice the shape. The error is zero at the centre and grows as the cube of the radius. Anything
you check by looking at the middle of the image will look perfect.

### Level 2 — the nine numbers

`fx, fy` — focal length per axis, different if the pixels are not square or the sensor is cropped.
`cx, cy` — the **principal point**, where the optical axis actually meets the sensor.
`k1, k2, k3` — radial distortion, of which `k1` does almost all the work. `p1, p2` — tangential
distortion, from the lens not being exactly parallel to the sensor. Nine unknowns.

The second row is the one people assume away. The principal point is never exactly the middle of
the pixel array — the lens is glued on by a machine with a tolerance. Setting $c_x, c_y = w/2,
h/2$ puts a fixed offset into every geolocation in [14.05](14.05-tracking-and-geolocation.md), and
a fixed offset is a **bias**, not a noise ([13.02](../13-navigation-gnss/13.02-error-sources.md)).

A calibration also returns one 6-DoF pose per image — the extrinsics, usually discarded — and a
per-point reprojection error, which is Level 5.

### Level 3 — why you must tilt the board

A calibration target is a plane. Photograph a plane head-on from distance $Z$ with focal length
$f$ and the image scale is $f/Z$. The code prints four completely different cameras — 1459 px at
0.5 m, 2918 at 1.0, 5836 at 2.0, 8754 at 3.0 — all producing an identical image.

A fronto-parallel plane cannot separate focal length from distance, and no number of images fixes
it if they are all square-on. **Tilt breaks the tie**: a tilted board is nearer at one edge than
the other, so the convergence of the rows depends on $f$ and $Z$ differently.

That is the entire reason every calibration guide tells you to wave the board around, and almost
none of them says why.

So the requirement is not a number of images. It is tilts in both axes up to about 45°, the board
in all four corners of the frame, a range of distances, and rotations about the optical axis —
the cheapest variety to add and the one everyone forgets. **Twenty good images beat two hundred
similar ones**, and a hundred head-on images are a beautifully converged fit to the wrong focal
length.

### Level 4 — how big a board, and the breathing trap

A 68.9° lens needs the board to fill most of the frame or the corners never get sampled. The frame
is 1.37 m wide at 1 m, so 80 % fill needs a **1.10 m board** — an A0 print on foam board, entirely
practical. At 5 m you would need 5.48 m of board, which is not.

So calibrate close. Which raises the thing that makes this different from a laboratory: **you
calibrated at 1 m and you fly at 60**.

For a fixed-focus lens that is fine — nothing moves, so the intrinsics are the intrinsics. For
anything that focuses it is not: focal length changes with focus distance ("breathing"), and a
calibration at 1 m describes a camera you are not flying. The fixes, in order of preference: use a
fixed-focus lens and tape any focus ring (this is why survey cameras are fixed); lock focus at
infinity and *then* calibrate, accepting a slightly soft board; or calibrate far against a large
measured target such as a building facade — awkward, and the most honest.

### Level 5 — the reprojection error is the only honest score

Calibration finds the parameters that best re-project the known 3-D corners onto the measured 2-D
corners. What is left over is the reprojection error, and it converts straight into ground metres:

| RMS reprojection | at 60 m | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 0.10 px | 0.2 cm | excellent — a careful set, sharp corners |
| **0.30 px** | **0.6 cm** | **the target** |
| 0.50 px | 1.0 cm | acceptable for mapping |
| 1.00 px | 2.1 cm | something is wrong — look per-image |
| 3.00 px | 6.2 cm | a blurred frame or a mis-detected corner |

Sub-pixel is not a boast, it is the requirement. At 0.30 px you place every pixel to 0.6 cm on the
ground, inside 12.02's GSD and therefore invisible. At 1.00 px you have added an error comparable
to the GSD itself.

And read it **per image**. A mean of 0.4 px can be nineteen images at 0.25 and one at 3.2, and that
one image is dragging the whole fit.

### Level 6 — the other half: where the camera is bolted

Intrinsics describe the camera. [14.05](14.05-tracking-and-geolocation.md) needs a
**camera-to-body transform**: a rotation and a translation from the airframe to the lens. The two
halves are not equally important.

| mount error | at 30 m | at 60 m | at 120 m |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5° of angle | 0.26 m | 0.52 m | 1.05 m |
| **1.0° of angle** | 0.52 m | **1.05 m** | 2.09 m |
| 5.0° of angle | 2.62 m | 5.25 m | 10.50 m |
| 5 cm of lever arm | 0.05 m | 0.05 m | 0.05 m |

The lever arm is a constant and the angle is a multiplier. At 60 m, one degree of mount error is
1.05 m — **twenty-one times** worse than a 5 cm lever arm you measured carefully with a ruler.
**Measure the angle, not the offset.**

And one degree is not a lot. It is the thickness of a washer under one corner of the mount, a
vibration damper that has taken a set, or a gimbal whose zero was never checked.
[14.03](14.03-gimbals-and-stabilisation.md) mounts it and 14.05 pays for any error here.

### Level 7 — undistortion is an iteration

The Brown–Conrady model has no closed-form inverse: you can distort an ideal point directly, but
recovering the ideal point from a measured one requires iterating. The code implements both and
checks closure across the frame — **worst case 6.8 × 10⁻⁷ pixels**.

It converges because the distortion is small compared with the coordinate. Which is also why it
*fails* on a fisheye, where it is not — and why fisheye lenses need a different projection model
entirely rather than a bigger `k3`.

> [!TIP]
> **Ask your teacher:** "What is our reprojection error, and when was the calibration done?" Two
> numbers, both on a file somewhere, and most teams cannot produce either. If the answer to the
> second is "before we changed the mount", the first one is fiction.

## Code

The focal length in pixels, the Brown–Conrady distortion evaluated across the frame and converted
to ground metres, the nine intrinsics enumerated, the scale ambiguity of a head-on plane shown
numerically, the board size needed at each distance, the reprojection-error conversion table, the
mount-angle-versus-lever-arm comparison, and a distort/undistort round-trip that closes to 10⁻⁷
pixels — all in pure Python, no OpenCV needed to run it.

```python
"""14.02 - what calibration is worth, in metres on the ground."""
import math

# 14.01's camera
PITCH = 6.17e-3 / 4000
FOCAL_M = 4.5e-3
PIX_W, PIX_H = 4000, 3000
FX = FOCAL_M / PITCH               # focal length in PIXELS
CX, CY = PIX_W / 2, PIX_H / 2
FOV_H = 2 * math.degrees(math.atan(6.17e-3 / (2 * FOCAL_M)))

# Brown-Conrady coefficients typical of a wide 1/2.3" module [S]
K1, K2, K3 = -0.250, 0.080, -0.012
P1, P2 = 0.0008, -0.0005

SURVEY_ALT = 60.0
GSD = PITCH * SURVEY_ALT / FOCAL_M

# the nine intrinsic unknowns, and what each one is
INTRINSICS = [
    ("fx, fy", 2, "focal length in pixels, per axis",
     "different if the pixels are not square, or the sensor is cropped"),
    ("cx, cy", 2, "the PRINCIPAL POINT",
     "where the optical axis actually hits the sensor. Never the centre"),
    ("k1, k2, k3", 3, "radial distortion",
     "the barrel or pincushion. k1 does almost all of it"),
    ("p1, p2", 2, "tangential distortion",
     "the lens not being parallel to the sensor. Small, and real"),
]

# the field procedure
STEPS = [
    ("print the board FLAT and measure it",
     "a warped board calibrates a warped lens. Glass or foam board, "
     "and measure a square with callipers -- printers lie by 1-2 %"),
    ("fill the frame, at the working distance you can manage",
     "section 4. The board has to be big or the distance small"),
    ("TILT IT. Every frame, a different tilt",
     "section 3: this is the step that makes the problem solvable"),
    ("put the board in EVERY part of the frame, especially the corners",
     "that is where section 1's 362 px live. A centre-only set "
     "calibrates the part that was already fine"),
    ("20 to 30 images, and throw away the blurred ones",
     "14.01's one-pixel rule applies to the calibration shots too"),
    ("check the REPROJECTION ERROR, per image, not just the mean",
     "one bad image hides in a mean and dominates a fit"),
    ("re-do it after any knock, any refocus, any lens change",
     "and write the DATE on the file"),
]


def distort(xn, yn, k1=K1, k2=K2, k3=K3, p1=P1, p2=P2):
    """Brown-Conrady forward: ideal normalised -> distorted normalised."""
    r2 = xn * xn + yn * yn
    rad = 1 + k1 * r2 + k2 * r2 * r2 + k3 * r2 ** 3
    xt = 2 * p1 * xn * yn + p2 * (r2 + 2 * xn * xn)
    yt = p1 * (r2 + 2 * yn * yn) + 2 * p2 * xn * yn
    return xn * rad + xt, yn * rad + yt


def undistort(xd, yd, iters=20, **kw):
    """The inverse has no closed form. Iterate -- which is what OpenCV does."""
    xn, yn = xd, yd
    for _ in range(iters):
        xp, yp = distort(xn, yn, **kw)
        xn += (xd - xp)
        yn += (yd - yp)
    return xn, yn


def px_to_norm(u, v):
    return (u - CX) / FX, (v - CY) / FX


def norm_to_px(xn, yn):
    return xn * FX + CX, yn * FX + CY


def board_width_needed(dist_m, fill=0.8, fov=FOV_H):
    return 2 * dist_m * math.tan(math.radians(fov / 2)) * fill


def bar(t):
    print("\n" + "=" * 70)
    print(t)
    print("=" * 70)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    bar("1. WHAT AN UNCALIBRATED LENS COSTS, IN METRES")
    print(f"  14.01 gave the pitch. Divide the focal length by it and you")
    print(f"  get the focal length IN PIXELS, which is what every vision")
    print(f"  equation actually uses:")
    print(f"  {'focal length':24s} {FOCAL_M * 1000:8.2f} mm")
    print(f"  {'pixel pitch':24s} {PITCH * 1e6:8.3f} um")
    print(f"  {'fx = f / pitch':24s} {FX:8.1f} px")
    print("  NOW THE DISTORTION. A wide lens bends straight lines, and")
    print("  the Brown-Conrady model says by how much. Walk out from the")
    print(f"  centre of a {PIX_W} x {PIX_H} frame:")
    print(f"  {'position in frame':24s} {'radius':>8s} {'shifted by':>12s}"
          f" {'on the ground':>15s}")
    for nm, u, v in (("dead centre", CX, CY),
                     ("quarter way out", CX + 500, CY + 375),
                     ("half way out", CX + 1000, CY + 750),
                     ("three quarters", CX + 1500, CY + 1125),
                     ("THE CORNER", PIX_W, PIX_H)):
        xn, yn = px_to_norm(u, v)
        xd, yd = distort(xn, yn)
        ud, vd = norm_to_px(xd, yd)
        shift = math.hypot(ud - u, vd - v)
        r = math.hypot(u - CX, v - CY)
        print(f"  {nm:24s} {r:6.0f} px {shift:9.1f} px"
              f" {shift * GSD:12.2f} m")
    xn, yn = px_to_norm(PIX_W, PIX_H)
    xd, yd = distort(xn, yn)
    ud, vd = norm_to_px(xd, yd)
    corner_px = math.hypot(ud - PIX_W, vd - PIX_H)
    print(f"  THE CORNER OF AN UNCALIBRATED FRAME IS {corner_px:.0f} PIXELS"
          f" OUT OF")
    print(f"  PLACE, WHICH AT 60 METRES IS {corner_px * GSD:.1f} METRES"
          f" ON THE GROUND.")
    print("  That is not a refinement. 13.03 sold you centimetres for two")
    print("  thousand shekels and an uncalibrated lens throws away seven")
    print("  metres in the corner of every frame -- for free, silently,")
    print("  and worst exactly where the overlap between adjacent survey")
    print("  images lives (12.02).")
    print("  AND NOTICE THE SHAPE: it is nothing at the centre and grows")
    print("  as the CUBE of the radius. Anything you check by looking at")
    print("  the middle of the image will look perfect.")

    bar("2. THE NINE NUMBERS, AND WHAT EACH ONE IS")
    n = 0
    for nm, cnt, what, why in INTRINSICS:
        n += cnt
        print(f"  {nm:12s} ({cnt}) {what}")
        print(f"  {'':18s} {why}")
    print(f"  {'':12s} ({n}) unknowns in total")
    print("  THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE PEOPLE ASSUME. The principal")
    print("  point is where the optical axis hits the sensor, and it is")
    print("  never exactly the middle of the pixel array -- the lens is")
    print("  glued on by a machine with a tolerance. Assuming cx, cy =")
    print("  w/2, h/2 puts a fixed offset into every geolocation in")
    print("  14.05, and a fixed offset is a BIAS, not a noise (13.02).")
    print("\n  AND WHAT A CALIBRATION ACTUALLY RETURNS BESIDES THOSE NINE:")
    for a, b in (("one 6-DoF pose per image",
                  "the EXTRINSICS: where the board was. Usually thrown "
                  "away, and section 5 needs the idea"),
                 ("a reprojection error, per point",
                  "the only honest quality measure you get")):
        print(f"    {a:30s} {b}")

    bar("3. WHY YOU MUST TILT THE BOARD")
    print("  A calibration target is a PLANE. Photograph a plane")
    print("  head-on, from distance Z, with focal length f, and the")
    print("  image scale is f/Z. Double both and NOTHING CHANGES.")
    print(f"  {'f (px)':>9s} {'Z (m)':>8s} {'f / Z':>10s} {'board in frame'}")
    for f_px, z in ((2918, 1.00), (5836, 2.00), (1459, 0.50), (8754, 3.00)):
        print(f"  {f_px:9.0f} {z:8.2f} {f_px / z:10.0f}   identical")
    print("  FOUR COMPLETELY DIFFERENT CAMERAS PRODUCE THE SAME IMAGE.")
    print("  A fronto-parallel plane cannot separate focal length from")
    print("  distance, and no number of images fixes it if they are all")
    print("  taken square-on.")
    print("  TILT BREAKS THE TIE. A tilted board is nearer at one edge")
    print("  than the other, so the PERSPECTIVE -- the convergence of the")
    print("  rows -- depends on f and Z differently. That is the entire")
    print("  reason every calibration guide tells you to wave the board")
    print("  around, and almost none of them says why.")
    print("\n  SO THE REQUIREMENT IS NOT A NUMBER OF IMAGES. IT IS:")
    for a in ("tilts in both axes, up to about 45 degrees",
              "the board in all four CORNERS of the frame, not just the "
              "middle",
              "a range of distances",
              "and rotations about the optical axis, which is the cheapest "
              "variety to add and the one everyone forgets"):
        print(f"    - {a}")
    print("  TWENTY GOOD IMAGES BEAT TWO HUNDRED SIMILAR ONES, and a")
    print("  hundred head-on images are a beautifully converged fit to")
    print("  the wrong focal length.")

    bar("4. HOW BIG A BOARD, AND AT WHAT DISTANCE")
    print(f"  A {FOV_H:.0f} degree lens needs the board to fill most of the")
    print("  frame, or the corners never get sampled:")
    print(f"  {'at this distance':>17s} {'the frame is':>14s}"
          f" {'board for 80 % fill':>21s}")
    for d in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0):
        print(f"  {d:15.1f} m {2 * d * math.tan(math.radians(FOV_H / 2)):11.2f} m"
              f" {board_width_needed(d):18.2f} m")
    print("  AT ONE METRE YOU NEED A ONE-METRE BOARD, which is an A0")
    print("  print on foam board and entirely practical. At five metres")
    print("  you need five metres of board, which is not.")
    print("  SO CALIBRATE CLOSE -- AND THEN WORRY ABOUT THE ONE THING")
    print("  THAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM A LABORATORY:")
    print("  YOU CALIBRATED AT 1 m AND YOU FLY AT 60 m.")
    print("  For a FIXED-FOCUS lens that is fine: nothing moves, so the")
    print("  intrinsics are the intrinsics. For anything that focuses,")
    print("  IT IS NOT -- the focal length changes with focus distance")
    print("  ('breathing'), and a calibration at 1 m describes a camera")
    print("  you are not flying.")
    print("  THE FIXES, IN ORDER OF PREFERENCE:")
    for a, b in (("use a fixed-focus lens", "and tape the focus ring if "
                  "it has one. This is why survey cameras are fixed"),
                 ("lock focus at infinity, then calibrate",
                  "the lens is then in the state it flies in, even if "
                  "the board is close and slightly soft"),
                 ("calibrate far, with a big target",
                  "a building facade with measured features. Awkward, "
                  "and the most honest")):
        print(f"    {a:34s} {b}")

    bar("5. THE REPROJECTION ERROR IS THE ONLY HONEST SCORE")
    print("  Calibration finds the parameters that best re-project the")
    print("  known 3-D corners onto the measured 2-D corners. What is")
    print("  left over is the reprojection error, in pixels -- and it")
    print("  converts straight into ground metres:")
    print(f"  {'RMS reprojection':>18s} {'at 60 m':>10s} {'verdict'}")
    for e, verdict in ((0.10, "excellent -- a careful set, sharp corners"),
                       (0.30, "GOOD. This is the target"),
                       (0.50, "acceptable for mapping"),
                       (1.00, "something is wrong. Look per-image"),
                       (3.00, "a blurred frame or a mis-detected corner")):
        print(f"  {e:15.2f} px {e * GSD * 100:7.1f} cm   {verdict}")
    print("  SUB-PIXEL IS NOT A BOAST, IT IS THE REQUIREMENT. At 0.30 px")
    print(f"  you are placing every pixel to {0.30 * GSD * 100:.1f} cm on the"
          f" ground, which is")
    print("  inside 12.02's GSD and therefore invisible. At 1.00 px you")
    print("  have added an error comparable to the GSD itself.")
    print("  AND READ IT PER IMAGE. A mean of 0.4 px can be nineteen")
    print("  images at 0.25 and one at 3.2, and that one image is")
    print("  dragging the whole fit. Throw it out and re-run.")

    print("  Intrinsics describe the camera. They say nothing about")
    print("  where it points. 14.05 needs a CAMERA-TO-BODY transform:")
    print("  a rotation and a translation from the airframe to the lens.")

    print(f"  {'mount error':>26s} {'at 30 m':>10s} {'at 60 m':>10s}"
          f" {'at 120 m':>10s}")
    for deg in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0):
        row = [SURVEY_ALT * 0 + h * math.tan(math.radians(deg))
               for h in (30, 60, 120)]
        print(f"  {f'{deg:.1f} deg of ANGLE':>26s} {row[0]:7.2f} m"
              f" {row[1]:7.2f} m {row[2]:7.2f} m")
    for cm in (2, 5, 10, 20):
        print(f"  {f'{cm} cm of LEVER ARM':>26s} {cm / 100:7.2f} m"
              f" {cm / 100:7.2f} m {cm / 100:7.2f} m")
    ratio = 60 * math.tan(math.radians(1)) / 0.05
    print("  THE LEVER ARM IS A CONSTANT AND THE ANGLE IS A MULTIPLIER.")
    print(f"  At 60 m, ONE DEGREE of mount error is"
          f" {60 * math.tan(math.radians(1)):.2f} m --"
          f" {ratio:.0f} times")
    print("  worse than a 5 cm lever arm you measured carefully with a")
    print("  ruler. MEASURE THE ANGLE, NOT THE OFFSET.")
    print("  AND ONE DEGREE IS NOT A LOT. It is the thickness of a washer")
    print("  under one corner of the mount, or a vibration damper that")
    print("  has taken a set, or a gimbal whose zero was never checked.")
    print("  14.03 mounts it and 14.05 pays for any error here.")

    bar("7. THE FIELD PROCEDURE, AND THE ROUND-TRIP TEST")
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(STEPS, 1):
        print(f"  {i}. {a}")
        print(f"     {b}")
    print("\n  AND A TEST YOU CAN RUN WITHOUT A CAMERA. The distortion")
    print("  model has no closed-form inverse, so undistorting is an")
    print("  iteration. Verify it closes:")
    print(f"  {'point':22s} {'distort -> undistort closes to':>32s}")
    worst = 0.0
    for nm, u, v in (("centre", CX + 1, CY + 1),
                     ("half way out", CX + 1000, CY + 750),
                     ("corner", PIX_W, PIX_H),
                     ("far corner, other side", 0, 0)):
        xn, yn = px_to_norm(u, v)
        xd, yd = distort(xn, yn)
        xr, yr = undistort(xd, yd)
        err_px = math.hypot(xr - xn, yr - yn) * FX
        worst = max(worst, err_px)
        print(f"  {nm:22s} {err_px:28.2e} px")
    print(f"  WORST CLOSURE {worst:.2e} PIXELS over the whole frame. The")
    print("  iteration converges because the distortion is small compared")
    print("  with the coordinate -- which is also why it FAILS on a")
    print("  fisheye, where it is not, and why fisheye lenses need a")
    print("  different model entirely.")
```

======================================================================
1. WHAT AN UNCALIBRATED LENS COSTS, IN METRES
======================================================================
  14.01 gave the pitch. Divide the focal length by it and you
  get the focal length IN PIXELS, which is what every vision
  equation actually uses:
  focal length                 4.50 mm
  pixel pitch                 1.542 um
  fx = f / pitch             2917.3 px
  NOW THE DISTORTION. A wide lens bends straight lines, and
  the Brown-Conrady model says by how much. Walk out from the
  centre of a 4000 x 3000 frame:
  position in frame          radius   shifted by   on the ground
  dead centre                   0 px       0.0 px         0.00 m
  quarter way out             625 px       7.0 px         0.14 m
  half way out               1250 px      54.0 px         1.11 m
  three quarters             1875 px     169.3 px         3.48 m
  THE CORNER                 2500 px     362.5 px         7.46 m
  THE CORNER OF AN UNCALIBRATED FRAME IS 362 PIXELS OUT OF
  PLACE, WHICH AT 60 METRES IS 7.5 METRES ON THE GROUND.
  That is not a refinement. 13.03 sold you centimetres for two
  thousand shekels and an uncalibrated lens throws away seven
  metres in the corner of every frame -- for free, silently,
  and worst exactly where the overlap between adjacent survey

  AND NOTICE THE SHAPE: it is nothing at the centre and grows

  the middle of the image will look perfect.

======================================================================
2. THE NINE NUMBERS, AND WHAT EACH ONE IS
======================================================================
  fx, fy       (2) focal length in pixels, per axis
                     different if the pixels are not square, or the sensor is cropped
  cx, cy       (2) the PRINCIPAL POINT
                     where the optical axis actually hits the sensor. Never the centre
  k1, k2, k3   (3) radial distortion
                     the barrel or pincushion. k1 does almost all of it
  p1, p2       (2) tangential distortion
                     the lens not being parallel to the sensor. Small, and real
               (9) unknowns in total
  THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE PEOPLE ASSUME. The principal
  point is where the optical axis hits the sensor, and it is
  never exactly the middle of the pixel array -- the lens is
  glued on by a machine with a tolerance. Assuming cx, cy =
  w/2, h/2 puts a fixed offset into every geolocation in
  14.05, and a fixed offset is a BIAS, not a noise (13.02).

  AND WHAT A CALIBRATION ACTUALLY RETURNS BESIDES THOSE NINE:
    one 6-DoF pose per image       the EXTRINSICS: where the board was. Usually thrown away, and section 5 needs the idea
    a reprojection error, per point the only honest quality measure you get

======================================================================
3. WHY YOU MUST TILT THE BOARD
======================================================================
  A calibration target is a PLANE. Photograph a plane
  head-on, from distance Z, with focal length f, and the
  image scale is f/Z. Double both and NOTHING CHANGES.
     f (px)    Z (m)      f / Z board in frame
       2918     1.00       2918   identical
       5836     2.00       2918   identical
       1459     0.50       2918   identical
       8754     3.00       2918   identical
  FOUR COMPLETELY DIFFERENT CAMERAS PRODUCE THE SAME IMAGE.
  A fronto-parallel plane cannot separate focal length from
  distance, and no number of images fixes it if they are all
  taken square-on.
  TILT BREAKS THE TIE. A tilted board is nearer at one edge
  than the other, so the PERSPECTIVE -- the convergence of the
  rows -- depends on f and Z differently. That is the entire
  reason every calibration guide tells you to wave the board
  around, and almost none of them says why.

  SO THE REQUIREMENT IS NOT A NUMBER OF IMAGES. IT IS:
    - tilts in both axes, up to about 45 degrees
    - the board in all four CORNERS of the frame, not just the middle
    - a range of distances
    - and rotations about the optical axis, which is the cheapest variety to add and the one everyone forgets
  TWENTY GOOD IMAGES BEAT TWO HUNDRED SIMILAR ONES, and a
  hundred head-on images are a beautifully converged fit to
  the wrong focal length.

======================================================================
4. HOW BIG A BOARD, AND AT WHAT DISTANCE
======================================================================
  A 69 degree lens needs the board to fill most of the
  frame, or the corners never get sampled:
   at this distance   the frame is   board for 80 % fill
              0.5 m        0.69 m               0.55 m
              1.0 m        1.37 m               1.10 m
              2.0 m        2.74 m               2.19 m
              5.0 m        6.86 m               5.48 m
             10.0 m       13.71 m              10.97 m
  AT ONE METRE YOU NEED A ONE-METRE BOARD, which is an A0
  print on foam board and entirely practical. At five metres
  you need five metres of board, which is not.
  SO CALIBRATE CLOSE -- AND THEN WORRY ABOUT THE ONE THING
  THAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM A LABORATORY:
  YOU CALIBRATED AT 1 m AND YOU FLY AT 60 m.
  For a FIXED-FOCUS lens that is fine: nothing moves, so the
  intrinsics are the intrinsics. For anything that focuses,
  IT IS NOT -- the focal length changes with focus distance
  ('breathing'), and a calibration at 1 m describes a camera
  you are not flying.
  THE FIXES, IN ORDER OF PREFERENCE:
    use a fixed-focus lens             and tape the focus ring if it has one. This is why survey cameras are fixed
    lock focus at infinity, then calibrate the lens is then in the state it flies in, even if the board is close and slightly soft
    calibrate far, with a big target   a building facade with measured features. Awkward, and the most honest

======================================================================
5. THE REPROJECTION ERROR IS THE ONLY HONEST SCORE
======================================================================
  Calibration finds the parameters that best re-project the
  known 3-D corners onto the measured 2-D corners. What is
  left over is the reprojection error, in pixels -- and it
  converts straight into ground metres:
    RMS reprojection    at 60 m verdict
             0.10 px     0.2 cm   excellent -- a careful set, sharp corners
             0.30 px     0.6 cm   GOOD. This is the target
             0.50 px     1.0 cm   acceptable for mapping
             1.00 px     2.1 cm   something is wrong. Look per-image
             3.00 px     6.2 cm   a blurred frame or a mis-detected corner
  SUB-PIXEL IS NOT A BOAST, IT IS THE REQUIREMENT. At 0.30 px
  you are placing every pixel to 0.6 cm on the ground, which is
  inside 12.02's GSD and therefore invisible. At 1.00 px you
  have added an error comparable to the GSD itself.
  AND READ IT PER IMAGE. A mean of 0.4 px can be nineteen
  images at 0.25 and one at 3.2, and that one image is
  dragging the whole fit. Throw it out and re-run.

======================================================================
6. THE OTHER HALF: WHERE THE CAMERA IS BOLTED
======================================================================
  Intrinsics describe the camera. They say nothing about
  where it points. 14.05 needs a CAMERA-TO-BODY transform:
  a rotation and a translation from the airframe to the lens.
  AND THE TWO HALVES ARE NOT EQUALLY IMPORTANT:
                 mount error    at 30 m    at 60 m   at 120 m
            0.5 deg of ANGLE    0.26 m    0.52 m    1.05 m
            1.0 deg of ANGLE    0.52 m    1.05 m    2.09 m
            2.0 deg of ANGLE    1.05 m    2.10 m    4.19 m
            5.0 deg of ANGLE    2.62 m    5.25 m   10.50 m
           2 cm of LEVER ARM    0.02 m    0.02 m    0.02 m
           5 cm of LEVER ARM    0.05 m    0.05 m    0.05 m
          10 cm of LEVER ARM    0.10 m    0.10 m    0.10 m
          20 cm of LEVER ARM    0.20 m    0.20 m    0.20 m
  THE LEVER ARM IS A CONSTANT AND THE ANGLE IS A MULTIPLIER.
  At 60 m, ONE DEGREE of mount error is 1.05 m -- 21 times
  worse than a 5 cm lever arm you measured carefully with a

  AND ONE DEGREE IS NOT A LOT. It is the thickness of a washer
  under one corner of the mount, or a vibration damper that

  14.03 mounts it and 14.05 pays for any error here.

======================================================================

======================================================================
  1. print the board FLAT and measure it
     a warped board calibrates a warped lens. Glass or foam board, and measure a square with callipers -- printers lie by 1-2 %
  2. fill the frame, at the working distance you can manage
     section 4. The board has to be big or the distance small
  3. TILT IT. Every frame, a different tilt

  4. put the board in EVERY part of the frame, especially the corners

  5. 20 to 30 images, and throw away the blurred ones

  6. check the REPROJECTION ERROR, per image, not just the mean

  7. re-do it after any knock, any refocus, any lens change
     and write the DATE on the file

  far corner, other side                     6.82e-07 px
  WORST CLOSURE 6.82e-07 PIXELS over the whole frame. The
  iteration converges because the distortion is small compared
  with the coordinate -- which is also why it FAILS on a
  fisheye, where it is not, and why fisheye lenses need a

## Exercise

### Exercise 14.02-E1 — Calibrate it, properly `[build]`

Print a checkerboard, mount it flat, **measure a square with callipers**, and shoot 25 images with
real variety: tilts in both axes, all four corners, a range of distances, and rotations about the
optical axis. Run OpenCV's `calibrateCamera` and report `fx, fy, cx, cy`, the five distortion
coefficients, and the RMS reprojection error.

### Exercise 14.02-E2 — Compare against the spec sheet `[analysis]`

Compare your measured `fx` against 14.01's `focal / pitch`, and your measured `cx, cy` against the
image centre. Convert both discrepancies into ground metres at your survey altitude.

### Exercise 14.02-E3 — Prove the tilt matters `[build]`

Calibrate twice from the same session: once using only your most head-on images, once using only
your most tilted ones. Compare the focal lengths and the reported errors. Then decide which one
you believe, and why.

### Exercise 14.02-E4 — Undistort a real frame and measure the corner `[build]`

Take one aerial frame with a straight feature running through a corner — a road edge, a fence,
a field boundary. Undistort it with your coefficients and measure how far the corner moved, in
pixels and then in ground metres at the altitude you flew.

## Expected result

**14.02-E1**: expect `fx` within a few per cent of `focal / pitch`, `cx, cy` offset from the
centre by tens of pixels, and an RMS error between 0.15 and 0.5 px. If your error is under 0.1 px
with only fifteen images, be suspicious rather than pleased — it usually means too little variety
and an over-fitted model.

**14.02-E2**: the `cx, cy` offset is the interesting one. Tens of pixels is normal; at 60 m and
2.06 cm GSD, 40 px is 0.8 m of constant, directional offset in every geolocation you ever compute.

**14.02-E3**: the head-on set should give a focal length that is both different and confidently
reported, which is the lesson — a small reprojection error tells you the model fits the data, not
that the data could determine the model.

**14.02-E4**: expect a corner movement of a few hundred pixels and a few metres on the ground,
matching Level 1's order of magnitude. The straight feature should end up straight, which is the
visual confirmation that the numbers are right.

## Troubleshooting

**`calibrateCamera` fails to find corners.** Usually contrast or blur. Light the board evenly,
avoid glare, and apply 14.01's one-pixel rule to the calibration shots too.

**Reprojection error is high on a few images only.** Those images are the problem, not the model.
Inspect them — a warped board, a mis-detected corner, or motion blur — and re-run without them.

**Every image has a high error.** Usually a wrong board geometry: the square size you typed does
not match the square you printed. Printers scale by 1–2 % routinely. Measure with callipers.

**The focal length looks wrong but the error is tiny.** Level 3. All your images were head-on and
the fit is confidently under-determined.

**The undistorted image has a curved border.** Correct and expected. The rectangle you started with
was a distorted view of a curved region; straightening it curves the edges.

**Calibration was good and geolocation is still off by a metre.** Level 6. Check the mount angle
before you re-calibrate the lens.

**Results changed after re-mounting the camera.** The intrinsics should not have. If they did, the
mount is stressing the lens barrel — which is worth knowing, and worth fixing mechanically.

## Common mistakes

- **Checking distortion by looking at the middle of the image.** It grows as r³; the middle is
  always fine.
- **Assuming the principal point is the image centre.** It is a bias in every subsequent
  geolocation.
- **Shooting all the calibration images head-on.** Scale-ambiguous, and it fails confidently.
- **Not filling the frame.** The corners are the whole point and an unsampled corner is
  extrapolated.
- **Trusting the printed square size.** Measure it.
- **Calibrating a lens that will be refocused before flight.** Breathing.
- **Reporting only the mean reprojection error.** One bad frame dominates a fit and hides in a
  mean.
- **Measuring the lever arm carefully and eyeballing the angle.** The angle is 21× more
  important.

## Knowledge check

<details>
<summary>How far out of place is the corner of an uncalibrated frame, and why does it not show up
in casual inspection?</summary>

About 362 pixels, which is 7.46 m on the ground at 60 m. It does not show up because radial
distortion grows as the cube of the radius — it is zero at the centre, 7 px a quarter of the way
out, and everything happens in the outer quarter that nobody examines.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Why is assuming `cx, cy = w/2, h/2` a bias rather than a noise?</summary>

Because the offset is fixed — the lens is glued to the sensor at whatever position the machine
achieved, and it does not change from frame to frame. Every geolocation in 14.05 inherits the same
directional error, so averaging more frames makes the wrong answer more precise.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Explain, with numbers, why a head-on calibration cannot determine the focal length.</summary>

The image scale of a fronto-parallel plane is f/Z. A 1459 px lens at 0.5 m, a 2918 px lens at 1 m
and a 5836 px lens at 2 m all give 2918 — identical images. Nothing in the data distinguishes
them, so the fit converges, reports a small error, and is wrong.
</details>

<details>
<summary>What does tilting the board actually add?</summary>

Perspective. A tilted board is genuinely nearer at one edge than the other, so the convergence of
its rows depends on focal length and distance in *different* ways — which breaks the f/Z
degeneracy. Tilts in both axes, plus rotation about the optical axis, plus corner coverage, is the
real requirement; image count is not.
</details>

<details>
<summary>You have a 68.9° lens and want 80 % frame fill at 1 m. How big a board, and why not
calibrate at 5 m instead?</summary>

1.10 m — an A0 print on foam board. At 5 m you would need 5.48 m of board, which is impractical.
The consequence is that you calibrate close and fly far, which is only safe with a fixed-focus
lens or with focus locked at infinity before calibrating.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Your calibration reports 1.00 px RMS. Is that good?</summary>

No. At 60 m it is 2.1 cm on the ground — comparable to the GSD itself, so you have added an error
the size of your resolution. The target is 0.30 px (0.6 cm), and a 1.00 px result usually means one
or two bad images rather than a uniformly poor set, so look per-image before re-shooting.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Why does one degree of mount angle matter twenty-one times more than 5 cm of lever
arm?</summary>

Because the lever arm is a constant offset — 5 cm at any altitude — while the angle is a
multiplier: 60 m × tan(1°) = 1.05 m, and 2.09 m at 120 m. Measuring the offset carefully while
eyeballing the angle is optimising the wrong term, and one degree is about one washer under one
corner of the mount.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Why is undistortion an iteration, and when does the iteration break?</summary>

Because Brown–Conrady maps ideal to distorted in closed form but not the reverse, so you refine an
estimate until it converges — to about 10⁻⁷ px here. It converges only while the distortion is
small relative to the coordinate, which is false for a fisheye; fisheyes need a different
projection model, not a larger `k3`.
</details>

## Practical challenge

Calibrate Hermon's camera and produce the file every later lesson will load.

1. Build a proper target: checkerboard on a rigid flat backing, squares measured with callipers.
2. Set the camera to exactly the resolution and mode you will fly, and lock the focus.
3. Shoot 25–30 images with deliberate variety and log which ones you shot for which reason.
4. Calibrate, and record the per-image reprojection error alongside the mean.
5. Throw out anything over 1 px, re-run, and note how much the parameters moved. If they moved a
   lot, your set was not varied enough.
6. Measure the camera-to-body rotation — not just the translation — with the aircraft levelled and
   a known distant target. Record it in degrees, with a method.
7. Undistort one real aerial frame and measure the corner shift against Level 1's prediction.
8. Save everything as one dated file: intrinsics, distortion, the transform, the RMS error, the
   date, and the camera's serial or a photograph of the exact assembly.

Step 8's photograph is not a joke. Six months from now the only way to know whether this
calibration still applies is to compare the assembly in front of you with the one it was measured
on.

## You can skip this if

You can calibrate Hermon's camera to a sub-pixel reprojection error and express the camera-to-body
transform. "Express" means as numbers in a file with a date, not as an intention.

## Go deeper

- OpenCV's camera calibration tutorial, which is the implementation everybody uses and the source
  of the Brown–Conrady conventions in this lesson:
  <https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/dc/dbb/tutorial_py_calibration.html>
- Zhang's method, the 2000 paper that made planar-target calibration practical and explains the
  degeneracy in Level 3 formally: <https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/a-flexible-new-technique-for-camera-calibration/>
- Kalibr, for the harder case of calibrating a camera *and* an IMU together, which is where
  14.05's transform ultimately wants to come from: <https://github.com/ethz-asl/kalibr>

**Version-sensitive:** OpenCV's calibration flags and the ordering of the distortion coefficient
vector have changed between major versions, and the fisheye model lives in a separate namespace.
Check the signature in the version you have installed rather than copying a snippet.

## Progress checkpoint

You can now state what an uncalibrated lens costs in ground metres, name the nine intrinsics and
say which one people wrongly assume, explain why a tilted board is a mathematical requirement
rather than folklore, read a reprojection error as a distance, and say why the mount angle
dominates the lever arm.

damping that kills 14.01's jello, and the shutter-speed rule that survives a moving aircraft.
